title: PowerShell Quick Reference
description: Look up a lesson idea, see its small example, and check a common mistake. Open the linked lesson for setup and practice steps.

entries.name: Print a greeting
entries.summary: Write-Output sends a value to the output stream. Here it appears in the terminal.
notes: Write-Output sends data; Write-Host is mainly for host display.

entries.name: Keep a named value
entries.summary: PowerShell variable names start with a dollar sign.
notes: Use parentheses when passing a calculation as one argument.

entries.name: Build a message
entries.summary: Double-quoted strings expand variables inside the text.
notes: Single quotes keep the dollar text literal.

entries.name: Choose an action
entries.summary: -ge compares numbers using greater-than-or-equal. if chooses a block.
notes: PowerShell comparisons use names such as -eq and -ge.

entries.name: Read an array item
entries.summary: An array holds several values. Its first index is zero.
notes: Use @() when you need an array shape even with one item.

entries.name: Visit every item
entries.summary: foreach runs its block for each value in a group.
notes: The loop variable holds one item, not the whole group.

entries.name: Read a named key
entries.summary: A hashtable pairs keys with values. Brackets select a value by key.
notes: Separate hashtable entries with a semicolon or a new line.

entries.name: Make named properties
entries.summary: A custom object groups properties. Dot notation reads a property.
notes: Object properties and a formatted display are not the same thing.

entries.name: Filter pipeline values
entries.summary: Where-Object keeps values that pass a rule. $_ means the current pipeline item.
notes: Write the rule inside a script block with braces.

entries.name: Transform pipeline values
entries.summary: ForEach-Object runs a block for each incoming value.
notes: Use $_ for the current item inside the pipeline block.

entries.name: Name reusable steps
entries.summary: A function can declare inputs with param. An unassigned expression becomes output.
notes: Extra expressions in a function can also become output.

entries.name: Handle a terminating error
entries.summary: try and catch handle a terminating error. throw creates one here.

example.code: try { throw "Missing score" } catch { Write-Output "Try again" }

notes: Many command errors need -ErrorAction Stop to be caught by try/catch.
